cross_tool_domains.attrition: Serious risk: From a national frame of 1,103 delimited municipalities (3,309 potential municipality-period observations across three mayoral terms; 2,878 coverage observations in Table A1), estimation samples drop without missing-data adjustment or sensitivity testing to 767-893 municipalities (1,631-2,188 observations in Tables 6-7), losing ~30% of all municipalities in rural sewerage regressions and ~38% of large/medium municipalities (dropping from 61 in Table 4 to 37-38 in Tables 6-7).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious risk: Causal identification relies on internal Hausman-Taylor instruments whose exogeneity classifications were modified post hoc through iterative specification searches—reclassifying 2016-2019 administrative performance (MDM) and homicide rates as strictly exogenous instruments (pp. 18-19)—while omitting direct central-government municipal spending (Footnote 3, p. 9), Departmental Water Plans (PDA), private vs. public/community utility structure under Law 142, and common period shocks; Sargan-Hansen overidentification tests also fail in total coverage models (Tables 6-7, cols. 1 and 4).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate quality: The national decentralization and water-sector legal framework (1991 Constitution, Laws 60/1993, 142/1994, 617/2000, and 1176/2007 SGP-APSB earmark and tariff-subsidy rules) is accurately described and fiscal transfers/revenues are measured in real per-capita terms from official DNP/CGR accounts, but municipal administrative capacity (MDM) is back-imputed from 2016-2019 onto 2008-2015 and municipal provider legal forms (ESP, EICE, community aqueducts, PDA membership) are not operationalized in the regressions.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Serious risk: Fiscal and electoral indicators come from standardized administrative registries (DNP/CEDE, CGR, RNEC), but the administrative decentralization exposure (MDM) was only available starting in 2016 and was averaged over 2016-2019 and imputed backward across 2008-2015 as time-invariant (pp. 16-17, 23), introducing backward measurement error and post-outcome contamination; SSPD-REC outcome records also exclude non-conventional/community rural water systems (Footnote 4, p. 10).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate quality: Urban, rural, and total municipal aqueduct and sewerage coverage rates are drawn from official SSPD-REC administrative filings across 2008-2019 and log-normalized for boundedness (p. 14), but REC only counts residential connections served by formal conventional providers—systematically excluding ~25,500 community-managed/alternative rural providers (Footnote 4, p. 10; p. 25)—and captures nominal connection coverage rather than potability, continuity, or wastewater treatment quality.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Serious risk: No pre-analysis plan or protocol was registered, and the author explicitly describes multi-round specification searches ('aprendizaje estadístico', pp. 16, 18-19) across combinations of fiscal, political, and control variables—retaining variables (e.g., turnout only in rural sewerage; population density in Table 6 vs. rurality index in Table 7) and reclassifying endogenous/exogenous status based on statistical significance, sign stability, and passing post-estimation tests—while omitting fixed-effects and random-effects estimates (Footnote 9, p. 19).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate risk: All 1,103 Colombian municipalities delimited via digital elevation models were included in the target frame at the 2008 onset of the Law 1176/2007 SGP-APSB transfer regime, but entry into the analytic panel required reporting in SSPD's REC (which covers formal conventional providers rather than informal/community rural systems) and evaluates prevalent municipal decentralization structures established in the 1990s rather than new initiators.

domain_ratings.justification: The study estimates causal effects of fiscal, political, and administrative decentralization using a three-period Hausman-Taylor (HT) internal-IV panel model (2008-2011, 2012-2015, 2016-2019). However, HT consistency depends on strict exogeneity of designated time-varying and time-invariant exogenous regressors with respect to unobserved municipal heterogeneity. Through iterative specification searches (pp. 18-19), the author reclassified post-2016 municipal management performance (MDM, averaged over 2016-2019) from endogenous to time-invariant exogenous, using it alongside armed conflict (homicide rate) and geography to instrument fiscal revenues and electoral turnout. Treating municipal administrative management (measured at the end of the panel) and local homicide rates as uncorrelated with unobserved local institutional governance is implausible. Moreover, key time-varying confounders are omitted, including direct central-government sectoral spending in municipalities (explicitly noted as unavailable in Footnote 3, p. 9), Departmental Water Plans (PDA, p. 6), private vs. public utility governance under Law 142 (p. 7), and period fixed effects, while Sargan-Hansen overidentification tests reject instrument validity in total coverage models (Table 6 col. 4, p = 0.0386; Table 7 cols. 1 & 4, p < 0.001).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 9 (Footnote 3), 14-19 (Metodología empírica & Resultados econométricos), and 20-22 (Tables 6-7)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: The study defines a comprehensive national spatial frame of 1,103 Colombian municipalities using digital elevation models (p. 10) starting in 2008, coinciding with implementation of the Law 1176/2007 SGP-APSB transfer reform (p. 4). However, Colombia's broader fiscal, political, and regulatory decentralization began in the 1990s (prevalent exposure prior to follow-up), and inclusion in the coverage panel depended on municipal service providers filing in SSPD's REC system, which covers formal conventional utilities and excludes municipalities/areas served exclusively via community self-supply (Footnote 4, p. 10). Additionally, conditioning on backward-imputed 2016-2019 MDM scores introduces adjustment for a variable measured at the end of follow-up.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4 (Introducción), 6-7 (La experiencia colombiana), 10 (Table 3 & Footnote 4), and 16-17 (Bases de datos)

domain_ratings.justification: While fiscal exposures (SGP-water transfers, property tax, total tax revenue, royalties per capita in constant 2015 pesos) and municipal electoral indicators (ENP, top-two vote share, turnout) are measured contemporaneously from official DNP/CEDE, CGR, and RNEC administrative records averaged over each four-year mayoral term (pp. 16-17), the administrative decentralization exposure (MDM-gestión) was unavailable prior to 2016 because the earlier IDI index (2006-2016) was discontinued and non-comparable (pp. 16-17, Footnote 7). To fill 2008-2011 and 2012-2015, the author computed each municipality's 2016-2019 MDM average and imputed it backward as a time-invariant regressor across all three periods (p. 17). Classifying 2008-2015 municipal administrative capacity using 2016-2019 post-period scores introduces backward misclassification that can be directly influenced by prior infrastructure performance and fiscal trajectories, a limitation the author acknowledges as producing ambiguous coefficients (p. 23).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 16-17 (Bases de datos socioeconómicas y políticas & Footnote 7) and 23 (Resultados y discusión)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: As an observational panel evaluation of realized municipal fiscal revenues, transfers, electoral participation, and administrative capacity, experimental protocol adherence does not apply directly, but unbalanced co-interventions outside municipal budgets were active during 2008-2019 and unmeasured in the regressions—specifically direct national-budget water/sanitation investments in municipalities (Footnote 3, p. 9, citing ~11% national budget share in sector funding), Departmental Water Plans (PDA co-financing and coordination since 2007, p. 6), and emerging regional water markets after 2017 serving 58 municipalities (p. 25). Furthermore, Law 1176/2007 requires category 2-6 municipalities to allocate at least 15% of SGP-APSB transfers to demand-side tariff subsidies rather than infrastructure expansion (p. 7 & Footnote 1), which varies across municipalities above the statutory floor.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 6-7 (La experiencia colombiana & Footnote 1), 9 (Footnote 3), and 25 (Resultados y discusión)

domain_ratings.justification: Across 1,103 delimited municipalities and 3 mayoral periods (3,309 potential municipality-period cells; 2,878 coverage observations in Table A1, p. 30), regression samples in Tables 6 and 7 shrink substantially and unequally across specifications: aqueduct regressions retain 2,188 total observations (893 municipalities), 1,747 urban observations (802 municipalities), and 1,948 rural observations (860 municipalities); sewerage regressions retain 2,179 total observations (877 municipalities), 1,848 urban observations (823 municipalities), and only 1,631 rural observations (767 municipalities—losing 30% of Colombian municipalities and half of potential panel cells). Among the 61 large/medium municipalities in Table 4 (p. 12), only 37-38 municipalities (85-96 observations) appear in Tables 6-7 (cols. 7-9). Log transformations of zero-valued coverage/fiscal cells (Min = 0 in Table A1) and incomplete REC/fiscal reporting likely drive these exclusions, and no missing-data diagnostics, multiple imputation, or inverse-probability weighting are reported.

Outcomes (municipal total, urban, and rural aqueduct and sewerage coverage rates) come from SSPD's official administrative registry (Reporte de Estratificación y Cobertura, REC), preventing investigator subjectivity. However, Footnote 4 (p. 10) explicitly notes that REC measures only conventional residential connections supplied by registered service providers and excludes self-managed or alternative solutions (autogestión), diverging from DANE household survey coverage. Because approximately 25,500 community organizations provide water/sanitation services—predominantly in rural and remote municipalities (p. 25)—and official sector reports note persistent information-system gaps across diverse providers (p. 24), REC coverage entails systematic differential undercounting in rural/small municipalities relative to formalized urban systems.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 10 (Table 3 & Footnote 4), 14 (Metodología empírica), and 24-25 (Resultados y discusión)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of the reported result
domain_ratings.justification: No pre-analysis plan or study protocol is mentioned. In the Methods and Econometric Results sections (pp. 16, 18-19), the author explicitly reports conducting multiple rounds of estimations per dependent variable across varying combinations of decentralization indicators, control variables, and endogeneity classifications ('proceso de aprendizaje estadístico'), retaining specifications whose coefficient signs and p-values were 'robust' and passed Hausman and Sargan-Hansen post-estimation tests. Consequently, reported models vary across tables and columns without pre-specified rules: property tax (Lnpredia) is reported in urban/total columns while total tax revenue (Lntribut) replaces it in rural columns; municipal water spending (Gasto en agua) and competition metrics (enp, sumrank2) are dropped; voter turnout (Lnturnout) is included solely in rural sewerage (Table 7, cols. 3, 6, 9); Table 6 controls for population density whereas Table 7 controls for the rurality index; MDM was switched from endogenous to exogenous; and FE/RE benchmark tables are omitted ('disponibles a solicitud', Footnote 9, p. 19).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 16, 18-19 (Resultados econométricos y discusión & Footnote 9), 20 (Table 6), and 22 (Table 7)

overall_narrative_summary: Rojas Rivera (2026) conducts a comparative longitudinal panel evaluation of Colombian municipalities across three four-year mayoral terms (2008-2011, 2012-2015, 2016-2019), applying the Hausman-Taylor instrumental-variables panel estimator to assess the causal effects of fiscal, political, and administrative decentralization as well as municipal size and geographic region on urban and rural aqueduct and sewerage coverage. Appraised under ROBINS-I, the study has an overall Serious risk of bias driven by four domains rated Serious (D1 Confounding, D3 Classification of interventions, D5 Missing data, and D7 Selection of the reported result) and three rated Moderate (D2 Selection of participants, D4 Deviations from intended interventions, and D6 Measurement of outcomes). Specifically, (1) municipal administrative capacity (MDM) was unavailable before 2016 and was averaged over 2016-2019 and imputed backward across 2008-2015 as time-invariant (D3), then reclassified from endogenous to an exogenous Hausman-Taylor instrument during iterative specification searches (D1, D7); (2) central-government direct municipal water spending, Departmental Water Plans, utility privatization/provider legal forms under Law 142, and period fixed effects are omitted, and Sargan-Hansen tests fail in total-coverage models (D1, D4); (3) estimation samples lose 20%-30% of Colombia's 1,103 municipalities (and ~38% of large/medium municipalities) without missing-data adjustment (D5), while SSPD-REC outcome records systematically exclude ~25,500 rural/community self-managed water providers (D2, D6); and (4) reported regressors, control sets, and endogeneity assignments were selected post hoc across multiple estimation rounds based on coefficient significance, sign, and specification tests (D7).

why_tool_chosen: S385 is a non-randomized comparative longitudinal/panel econometric evaluation estimating causal effects of fiscal, political, and administrative decentralization policies across Colombian municipalities over 2008-2019 using the Hausman-Taylor panel instrumental-variables estimator. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, comparative longitudinal/panel and IV policy evaluations with continuous/categorical exposures across subnational jurisdictions map directly to ROBINS-I.
